requirements: The core contributions of 'LLM DNA: Tracing Model Evolution via Functional Representations' have been reproduced: the training-free RepTrace DNA extraction pipeline (Algorithm 1), DNA extraction across the 305-model pool, LLM relationship detection against the Hugging Face model tree, training-free model routing, the stability stress tests over heterogeneous prompts, random-word prompts and chat templates, the fine-tuning-intensity study, the Neighbor-Joining phylogenetic trees, and the appendix ablations over the bottleneck encoder, the embedding dimension p, the DNA dimension L, model scale, and the same-tokenizer regime, with results that align with the values and observations reported in the paper.

sub_tasks.requirements: The models, datasets, sentence-embedding encoders, generation settings, and compute environment required by the paper's experimental setting (Section 5.1, Appendix B, Appendix F) have been acquired and configured.
The evaluation pool of LLMs described in Section 5.1 and enumerated in Table 8 (Appendix F) has been assembled and made runnable.
All 305 LLMs enumerated in Table 8 (Appendix F) have been downloaded from Hugging Face or otherwise made accessible for inference, so that a response can be generated from each one.
The assembled model pool spans the 153 distinct releasing organizations reported in Section 5.1.
The assembled model pool includes decoder-only text-generation models (e.g., the GPT, Llama, and Qwen families), matching the 'Decoder Only' architecture entries in Table 8.

The assembled model pool includes encoder-decoder text-generation models (e.g., google-t5/t5-small, google-t5/t5-large, google/flan-t5-base, google/flan-t5-large), matching the 'Encoder Decoder' architecture entries in Table 8.
The assembled model pool covers the parameter range stated in Section 5.1, spanning models from roughly 100M parameters up to 70B parameters.
The assembled model pool includes base (completion) models, per Section 5.1.
The assembled model pool includes instruction-tuned models, per Section 5.1.
The six prompt-source benchmarks used for DNA extraction, plus the auxiliary datasets used for routing and fine-tuning experiments, have been acquired and prepared.
The SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.
The CommonsenseQA dataset (Talmor et al., 2018) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.
The HellaSwag dataset (Zellers et al., 2019) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.
The Winogrande dataset (Sakaguchi et al., 2020) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.
The ARC-Challenge dataset (Clark et al., 2018) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.
The MMLU dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021) has been acquired and made loadable for prompt sampling, per Section 5.1.

For each of the six benchmarks, prompts are read from that dataset's designated text field (e.g., 'question' for SQuAD/CommonsenseQA, 'sentence' for Winogrande, 'ctx' for HellaSwag) rather than from a concatenation of all fields, as specified in Section 5.1.

A single data-loading utility combines the six benchmarks into one prompt mixture that the DNA extraction pipeline consumes, implementing Section 5.1's statement that 'DNA extraction employs a mixture of all six datasets'.
Exactly 100 prompts are randomly sampled from each of the six benchmarks, so the default extraction prompt set contains 600 prompts in total, per Section 5.1.
The EmbedLLM dataset (Zhuang et al., 2025) has been acquired for the model-routing evaluation of Section 5.3.
The EmbedLLM dataset is excluded from the DNA extraction prompt mixture, per Section 5.1 ('though not involved in DNA extraction').
The NVIDIA OpenMathInstruct-2 dataset (Toshniwal et al., 2024) has been acquired for the fine-tuning-intensity experiment of Section 5.7.
The sentence-embedding encoders that act as the semantic bottleneck of RepTrace have been acquired and configured per Section 5.1 and Appendix B.1.
Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B has been acquired and configured as the default bottleneck sentence-embedding model for DNA extraction, per Section 5.1 and Appendix B.1.
sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 (0.1B parameters) has been acquired and configured as an alternative bottleneck sentence-embedding model, per Section 5.1.
BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 (0.3B parameters) has been acquired and configured as an alternative bottleneck sentence-embedding model, per Section 5.1.
The sentence-embedding model is invoked with a maximum input length of 1024 tokens, per Appendix B.1.
The sentence-embedding model uses CLS pooling to produce each fixed-size response embedding, per Appendix B.1.
The same sentence-embedding model used for DNA extraction is also used to encode the routing-experiment questions, preserving the semantic consistency required by Appendix B.1.
The text-generation configuration used to elicit each LLM's responses matches Appendix B.1.
Response generation uses max_length = 1024, per Appendix B.1.
Response generation uses temperature = 0.7, per Appendix B.1.
Response generation uses top_p = 0.9, per Appendix B.1.
All generation parameters not explicitly specified by the paper are left at their HuggingFace default values, per Appendix B.1 ('All other parameters follow HuggingFace defaults').
Models with fewer than 7B parameters are run in BF16/FP16 precision without quantization, per Appendix B.1.
Models larger than the 7B threshold are automatically quantized to 8-bit for memory efficiency, per Appendix B.1.
The protocol that turns a raw model generation into the response string fed to the embedding model matches Appendix B.1 and Appendix F.
For instruction-tuned models, the model-provided chat template is applied to the prompt by default, per Appendix B.1.
When a chat template is applied, only the assistant's response is extracted from the templated generation and used for DNA extraction, per Appendix B.1.
Any model-generated reasoning traces contained in an instruction-tuned model's response (e.g., Qwen3's thinking output) are retained as part of the response rather than stripped, per Appendix F.
For completion (base) models, the completed text itself is treated as the response used for DNA extraction, per Appendix F.
All applicable experiments are configured to run over five random seeds, with the mean and standard deviation of every reported metric recorded, per Appendix B.1.
The compute and storage environment matches the specification in Appendix B.2.
DNA extraction for each individual model is executed on a single GPU rather than being sharded across multiple GPUs, per Appendix B.2.
Models with up to 30B parameters are executed on an NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPU with 80GB of memory, per Appendix B.2.
Models between 30B and 70B parameters are executed on an NVIDIA H200 GPU with 140GB of memory, per Appendix B.2.
Storage capacity on the order of 20TB has been provisioned to hold the weights of all 305 models, consistent with the footprint reported in Appendix B.2.
The RepTrace DNA extraction pipeline of Algorithm 1 (Section 4.3, illustrated in Figure 1) has been implemented as a training-free, end-to-end procedure and executed over the model pool.
Each step of Algorithm 1 has been implemented.
Code exists to draw the sample input set S_t = {x_1, ..., x_t} uniformly from the real-world dataset mixture, supplying the prompt set that Algorithm 1 takes as input.
The default sample size is t = 600 prompts, obtained as 100 prompts from each of the six benchmarks, consistent with Section 5.1.
Code exists to feed each sampled prompt x_i to an LLM f and collect the textual response y_i = f(x_i), implementing line 4 of Algorithm 1.

Code exists to encode each textual response y_i into a fixed-size semantic embedding e_i = phi(y_i) in R^p using the sentence-embedding model phi, implementing line 5 of Algorithm 1 and the semantic-aware representation of Section 4.1.
Code exists to concatenate the t response embeddings end-to-end into a single functional representation E_f = [e_1, e_2, ..., e_t] in R^(p*t), implementing line 6 of Algorithm 1.
Code exists to initialize a random Gaussian projection matrix A of shape L x (p*t), implementing the shape requirement of line 1 of Algorithm 1 and Figure 1.
The entries of the projection matrix A are drawn i.i.d. as A_jk ~ N(0, 1/sqrt(L)), exactly as specified in line 1 of Algorithm 1.

The projection matrix A is pre-computed once outside the per-model loop and reused unchanged for every LLM in a given extraction run, so that all DNA vectors live in a common space, as required by the placement of line 1 before the foreach loop in Algorithm 1.
Code exists to compute the DNA vector tau_f = A * E_f in R^L, implementing line 7 of Algorithm 1.
The DNA dimensionality defaults to L = 128, the value used for all main experiments per Appendix B.1 and justified in Appendix C.5.
The implemented pipeline exhibits the design properties claimed for it in Sections 4.1 and 4.3.
No step of the DNA extraction pipeline performs gradient-based training or fine-tuning of any model or projection, satisfying the paper's 'training-free' claim in Section 4.3.
DNA extraction consumes only each LLM's generated text and requires no access to its internal architecture, weights, logits, or tokenizer, satisfying the LLM-agnostic benefit claimed in Section 4.1.

The extraction interface accepts a query-only (API-served) model as a valid input, so a closed-source LLM can have its DNA computed without local weights, satisfying the second benefit claimed in Section 4.1.

A newly added LLM's DNA can be computed without recomputing or altering the DNA vectors of previously processed LLMs, satisfying the third benefit claimed in Section 4.1 and overcoming EmbedLLM's fixed-model-set limitation.

Code exists to measure the functional distance between two LLMs as the Euclidean (L2) distance between their DNA vectors, serving as the computable estimate of the stochastic functional distance of Definition 4.1.
The RepTrace pipeline has been executed end-to-end over the full 305-model pool with the default configuration, producing one 128-dimensional DNA vector per model.

All methods compared in Table 1 have been implemented.
The Random baseline has been implemented, guessing 'correlated' or 'independent' uniformly at random for each pair, per Section 5.2.
The Greedy baseline has been implemented, predicting that every within-organization pair is correlated and every cross-organization pair is independent, per Section 5.2.

The PhyloLM baseline (Yax et al., 2025) has been implemented, computing Nei's genetic distance over output token distributions between models that share a tokenizer, per Section 5.2 and the Related Work description in Section 2.
The PhyloLM baseline handles models with differing tokenizers by approximating the distance from the first four characters of concatenated tokens, as described in Section 2.
For PhyloLM, each model's signature vector is formed from its genetic distances to the other LLMs in the training set, and this signature is the input to the downstream classifier, per Section 5.2.
An SVM with an RBF kernel is used as the downstream pair classifier for both PhyloLM and DNA, per Section 5.2.

The three observations Section 5.2 draws from Table 1 hold in the reproduction.

Every DNA variant outperforms the Random, Greedy, and PhyloLM + SVM baselines on the relationship-detection task, supporting Section 5.2's first observation that DNA significantly outperforms the baselines.
The best-performing DNA variant reaches an AUC of approximately 0.992, the headline figure quoted in Section 5.2.
For each of the three DNA variants, the reproduced Recall exceeds the reproduced Precision, supporting Section 5.2's second observation that unlabelled relationships exist in the official model tree.

The BGE (0.3B) and MPNet (0.1B) DNA variants achieve relationship-detection performance comparable to or better than the Qwen3-Embedding-8B variant despite their much smaller parameter counts, supporting Section 5.2's third observation that DNA quality is robust to the choice of sentence-embedding model.

The training-free model-routing experiment of Section 5.3, which drops frozen DNA vectors into the EmbedLLM matrix-factorization framework, has been reproduced (Table 2).
The routing framework and its variants have been implemented.

The EmbedLLM matrix-factorization routing framework (Zhuang et al., 2025) has been implemented or adapted, predicting whether a given model answers a given question correctly from the interaction between a model representation and a question representation.

Within that framework, the LLM embedding layer and its subsequent linear layer are together replaced by frozen pre-computed DNA vectors that receive no gradient updates during routing training, exactly as described in Section 5.3.
Routing questions are encoded with Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B and compared directly against the DNA vectors to make routing decisions, per Section 5.3 and Appendix B.1.
The routing experiment reuses EmbedLLM's own dataset, data split, baselines, and evaluation metric rather than defining new ones, per Section 5.3.
The 11 models reported by Zhuang et al. (2025) that no longer exist or fail to run are omitted from the routing model pool, per Section 5.3.
The reproduction records that, because of those omitted models, its routing numbers are not expected to align exactly with the numbers published by Zhuang et al. (2025), per Section 5.3.
The Random routing baseline has been implemented, selecting a model uniformly at random for each query.
The Single Best routing baseline has been implemented, always routing every query to the one model with the highest overall accuracy.
The original EmbedLLM baseline has been implemented, using EmbedLLM's own trainable (non-frozen) model embeddings inside the matrix-factorization framework.
Routing accuracy is computed as the fraction of queries routed to an LLM that answers them correctly, the definition attributed to Zhuang et al. (2025) in Section 5.3.
The routing evaluation has been executed on the EmbedLLM test split for all four methods, producing the numbers underlying Table 2.
The reproduced routing accuracies match those reported in Table 2.
The reproduced Table 2 entry for the Random routing baseline is 0.402 ± 0.016, matching the reported value within a reasonable tolerance.
The reproduced Table 2 entry for the Single Best routing baseline is 0.607 ± 0.000, matching the reported value within a reasonable tolerance.
The reproduced Table 2 entry for EmbedLLM (Matrix Factorisation) is 0.665 ± 0.003, matching the reported value within a reasonable tolerance.
The reproduced Table 2 entry for the DNA-based router is 0.672 ± 0.008, matching the reported value within a reasonable tolerance.

The reproduced routing accuracy of the frozen-DNA router exceeds that of the trained EmbedLLM embeddings, supporting Section 5.3's claim that a training-free, task-agnostic representation matches or beats a representation explicitly trained on this routing dataset.
The Section 5.4 Mantel-test experiment, which checks whether DNA structure depends on the prompt distribution used to extract it, has been reproduced (Figure 3).
The two disjoint prompt sets and the DNA vectors derived from them have been produced.
A prompt set named squad_cqa has been constructed as the union of 100 samples from SQuAD and 100 samples from CommonsenseQA, per Section 5.4.
A prompt set named hs_wg has been constructed as the union of 100 samples from HellaSwag and 100 samples from Winogrande, per Section 5.4.
The squad_cqa and hs_wg prompt sets are disjoint, drawing on four different source benchmarks with no shared prompts, as required by Section 5.4's description of 'two disjoint datasets'.
DNA vectors have been extracted for the same set of models twice, once using the squad_cqa prompts and once using the hs_wg prompts, yielding two independent DNA representations per model.
The Mantel-test analysis and its visualization have been implemented and executed.
Code exists to compute pairwise Euclidean distances between randomly selected pairs of models separately within the squad_cqa DNA set and within the hs_wg DNA set, per Section 5.4.
Code exists to compute the Pearson correlation and its p-value between the two vectors of pairwise model distances, implementing the Mantel test described in Section 5.4.
Code exists to render the Figure 3 scatter plot in which each point is one model pair, positioned by its squad_cqa distance on the horizontal axis and its hs_wg distance on the vertical axis.
The Figure 3 plot overlays a fitted regression line through the scatter of paired distances.
The Figure 3 plot carries an annotation box reporting the Pearson correlation and its p-value.
The full Mantel-test pipeline has been executed end-to-end to produce the results underlying Figure 3.
The reproduced Mantel-test statistics match those reported in Figure 3 and support the stability claim of Section 5.4.

The reproduced Pearson correlation between the squad_cqa and hs_wg pairwise distance structures is approximately 0.7797, the value annotated in Figure 3, matching the reported value within a reasonable tolerance.
The reproduced p-value for that correlation is below 0.0001, matching the significance level annotated in Figure 3.
The reproduced correlation is strong enough (Pearson r > 0.75 at p < 0.001) to support Section 5.4's conclusion that DNA structure does not depend on the sampled data from which it is extracted.
